messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kenji, a 22-year-old UX designer, presented as a quiet, observant young man who seemed to hold a significant amount of tension in his neck and shoulders. It has been fourteen months since the hiking trip that fundamentally altered his sense of safety and place in the world. He and his college friends were celebrating their graduation with a trip to a national park when a severe, unforecasted storm turned the canyon trail into a deathtrap. A flash flood descended with the sound of a freight train, a wall of brown water and debris that separated him from his friends in an instant. He remembers the shocking cold, the force that tore his grip from a tree root, and the violent, tumbling chaos underwater. For what felt like an eternity, he was tossed and submerged, his neck straining against the current as he fought to keep his head above the churning surface. The most persistent sensory memory is the taste: a horrifying slurry of mud, salt, and rot that filled his mouth and throat each time he was pulled under.

In the year since, Kenji has found that the trauma is not a static event in the past but an active presence in his daily life. The memories rarely arrive as a coherent narrative. More often, they are dismembered fragments. While sitting at his minimalist desk, designing a user flow for a new app, he will suddenly taste the grit and decay of the floodwater, a vivid sensation so powerful it makes him gag. Other times, with no warning, a wave of pure, undiluted terror will wash over him as he walks to the subway, his heart hammering against his ribs, but with no accompanying image to explain it. It is just the raw emotion of the event, untethered and terrifying. When he does try to consciously recall what happened, the story feels distant and absurd, like a special-effects-laden movie he once saw. He finds himself thinking, "That couldn't possibly have happened to me," a disbelief that leaves him feeling estranged from his own history.

These intrusive experiences are most often set off by seemingly benign physical sensations. A simple crick in his neck from leaning over his monitor for too long can instantly transport him back to the strain of fighting the current. A minor head cold or a bout of indigestion now carries a catastrophic weight; the feeling of being physically unwell is no longer just an inconvenience but a harbinger of the helplessness he felt in the water. At his open-plan office, he has learned to wear noise-cancelling headphones at all times, not for the ambient chatter, but to block out the breakroom television. The mere mention of floods or severe weather on the news is enough to make him feel unsteady for the rest of the day.

Over the months, these experiences have carved out a profound sense of alienation. He looks at his colleagues, laughing over a shared lunch or debating the merits of a new font, and feels as though he is watching a foreign species. Their concerns seem trivial, their world impossibly safe. He has come to believe that people are fundamentally unknowable, their friendly exteriors hiding a capacity for indifference he feels he witnessed in the chaotic aftermath of the flood. When his team lead invites him for coffee, he sees not kindness but a calculated professional maneuver. This deep-seated distrust has caused him to retreat, turning down social invitations and keeping his contributions in meetings brief and impersonal. He feels completely set apart, a survivor living in a different reality from everyone else. The world he belonged to before the flood is gone, and he is certain there is no place for him in this new one. It was after his manager gently noted his increasing disengagement and its impact on a team project that Kenji finally sought help, driven by a desperate, fading hope to find a way to belong somewhere again.
